You know, one of the craziest things I looked up recently were the historic tax rates. I highly encourage people to look at them here. When the US got into WW1 the highest tax rate jumped from 15% to 67%, then 77%, then back down to 73% for years. It wasn't until 1922 that the highest rate dropped significantly to 58% and then back down to 25% by 1926. Then in 1932 they jumped back up to 63%. Coincidentally this is when FDR set up The New Deal and originally funded Social Security. By the time World War II hit, in 1944 the highest tax rate had hit 94%. The highest tax bracket stayed north of 90% throughout the 50's, 70% in the 60's and 70's, 50% through some of the 80's, and mostly around 30%-40% through the present day.

What's the point of me saying all this? Our low tax rates are kind of insane and unprecedented. Back in the "good old days" the richest people in America payed north of 60% of their income in taxes, at a minimum.

And back then there were so many exceptions and loopholes, the effective tax rate was lower than it is now.

A list of historical tax rates without context is horribly misleading.

Expectations are important; managing expectations is key. A very important life skill - in relationships, at work, and certainly here.

Fattit isn't a "bad" place, but it has a certain function - /r/fitness in particular and loseit even more so - it's a positive attitude, can-do, motivational place.

If you want a pep talk, it's the perfect place. I think that sort of thing is a little hollow, so I don't frequent there often. But it's not the place where you can expect someone to say helpful things that may hurt your feelings.

People IRL too - as a society, we're trained to be polite to people; it's prioritized over being honest. Except for your closest friends and family, most likely.

You can get upset about it, but it's not something you can really change. Knowing what to expect from people will help you take a good perspective.

The person behind the counter at the gym is going to say something peppy and generic, your parents (well idk, mine anyway) are always going to say something positive and motivational. A large group of people is always going to focus on the positive.

So if you already know what they're going to say, what's the point of asking? Your energy may be better spent elsewhere.

Personal trainers aren't going to be judgey one way or the other - they'll ask you what your goals are and help you get there. If you already feel like you are x-amount overweight and want to lose x pounds, so you need as much feedback as you think you do?
